description: Hi! I’m Alex, a student passionate about space, CS, AI, and innovation. After competing in NASA Space Apps in Baku (2024, 2nd nationally & People’s Choice) and Mountain View, CA (2025), I’m leading Quantum Stack; a team of curious minds combining AI, coding, science, research, design, and storytelling. We’re looking for motivated teammates ready to experiment, collaborate, and think beyond the obvious. Join us! 🚀
summary: Crew Readiness is an offline, privacy-first software that lets crew members see whether they are working the way they usually do, before a critical operation such as docking. During a routine checklist it records only timing (how quickly and steadily someone types), never what is typed. Each check-in is compared with that person’s own past check-ins, not a population average, and any change is explained in plain words. The crew member sees their own result first, can add a short reaction check and private notes that never leave the device, and decides whether to involve a reviewer. A reminder flags missed check-ins, and the software tests its own health. It is a passive behavioural indicator that works without Earth, alongside physiological monitoring, not instead of it. We tested our method on real NASA bed-rest data, on simulated crews (false alerts fell from 13% to 4.7%) and with two volunteers. It is decision support, not diagnosis, and has never been tested on astronauts.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Crew Readiness is a working prototype of on-board decision support. It notices when a crew member is working differently from their own usual pattern, and puts that change in front of the person first, then a human reviewer, before a critical operation such as docking.

  1. Check-in. The crew member does a short, routine checklist: they read each step and type its fixed confirmation phrase (“CORRIDOR CLEAR”, “TARGET LOCK”). There are no sensors, wearables or extra tests.
  2. Timing only. The browser keeps timestamps, not keys. At the end it computes nine aggregate numbers (for example time between keystrokes, its spread, pauses of 2 s or more, time to start each step, corrections). The person sees exactly these numbers before anything is saved. Typed text, key identities and keystroke timelines never leave the device, and the server rejects them.
  3. Their own baseline. Each check-in is compared with that person’s earlier check-ins (median and robust spread), never with a population average, because 220 ms between keys is normal for one person and a large change for another. The first 5 check-ins only build the baseline and say nothing. Pause counts use a per-person count model, so one ordinary pause does not look alarming.
  4. A plain answer. GREEN, YELLOW or RED, with reasons in words (“a pause count this high would be expected about 1 session in 9”) and a suggested action: a short check-in, nothing more.
  5. The person first. “My check-in” shows the crew member their own status before anyone else. They can add an optional reaction check (10 trials, or a 3-minute version that follows the design of NASA’s Reaction Self Test), compared with their own earlier checks, and private notes (sleep, how they feel) that stay in their browser and are never sent.
  6. The reviewer. The reviewer views (Mission, the dashboard and a printable brief) show each role’s status and a review panel. Someone who is overdue is listed with “look in on them in person”; it says nothing is necessarily wrong. A step-by-step ladder shows who to involve next: self-check, a peer, the reviewer, crew medical support, the ground. No step is automatic. If a change is real and lasting (new gloves, a different device), a human accepts it as the new normal; the software never decides that itself.
  7. Built for isolation. It runs entirely on one computer with no internet. It checks its own health (database, scoring on a known example, clock, no outside network) and can back up and restore its data with a checksum. When a link to Earth opens, the crew can choose to send a short text summary of the aggregate numbers. Nothing is sent automatically.

BUILT ON REAL NASA DATA

We tested our method on NASA’s bed-rest study with the WinSCAT computer tests (NASA Life Sciences Data Archive, DOI 10.83263/sbne-th55): 24 people, 118 sessions before bed rest. About 65–87% of the difference in response speed is between people, which is why we compare each person only with themselves. At a 1-in-20 alert budget, the rule wrongly flagged 5.1% of normal sessions on people it had never seen. A single shared limit did about as well, so this checks our method; it does not prove the product works or say anything about anyone’s health. Our reaction check follows the design of NASA’s Reaction Self Test.

BENEFITS

  • The main check uses a routine the crew already does, so it adds no extra task.
  • Personal baselines suit people who differ, and they keep false alarms low. Crew time is scarce, and too many alarms teach people to ignore them.
  • Privacy by design: nine numbers, never text, and the crew member sees them first.
  • Explains itself in plain language, and always leaves the decision to a human.
  • Works fully offline, which suits missions with long communication delays.
  • A calculator on the Evidence page helps a planner estimate how many false alerts and how much reviewer time to expect for a given crew size and mission length.

INTENDED IMPACT

On long missions, isolation, workload and delayed contact with Earth make it harder to notice a change early. The intended impact is a private, low-effort self-check that helps a crew member and their team decide when to pause and talk before a critical operation, alongside existing health monitoring, not instead of it. The same idea could also suit other safety-critical work on Earth, such as aviation or control rooms, but we have not tested that.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • A passive behavioural signal from ordinary procedure work, measured against each person’s own pattern instead of a fixed threshold.
  • We found and fixed a flaw in the usual approach. In a sustained 20% simulated slowdown, a baseline that keeps learning absorbs the change, and detection falls from 0.88 to 0.07 by the fifteenth affected session. Keeping flagged sessions out of the baseline held it at 0.40, and a human decides when a genuine new normal starts. With new equipment, accepting the change cut repeated alerts from 27% to 11% of sessions (simulated).
  • A count model for pauses cut false alerts on normal sessions from about 13.0% to 4.7% at the product’s alert level (simulated, 300 people per row). We show the cost too: detection of a 10% slowdown fell from 0.42 to 0.35.
  • We publish what did not work: a “personal rarity” alert rule was calibrated but detected less, so we did not ship it.
  • A “stacked sessions” picture (inspired by the 1970 pulsar plot) shows a person’s history as lines that rise only where they differed from usual.

TOOLS

Python, Flask, SQLite and NumPy on the server; HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in the browser, with Chart.js and the fonts (Instrument Sans, Instrument Serif, JetBrains Mono, SIL Open Font License) stored locally so nothing loads from the internet. pytest (252 automated tests, including privacy and claims checks), Playwright browser checks for layout, keyboard use and phone width, axe-core for accessibility, Git and GitHub, and Vercel for the hosted demo. Hardware: an ordinary laptop and keyboard; no sensors. We used AI coding assistance (Claude); the team reviewed and owns every decision. No AI-generated images are used.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Privacy: only nine aggregate numbers are stored, the database has no column for text, and tests enforce it.
  • Honesty: it detects changes in interaction timing, not fatigue, illness or fitness for duty. Our evidence is real NASA bed-rest data, a simulated benchmark and a very small real check: two volunteers, where 5 of 6 deliberately changed sessions and 0 of 8 normal sessions were flagged. It has not been tested on astronauts, crews or in space, and the thresholds are illustrative.
  • False alarms and human judgement: a flag suggests a conversation; a person always decides.
  • Confounders: keyboard, language, time of day, sleep and practice can all change timing, and the page says so.
  • Accessibility and licences: keyboard use, contrast and phone width are checked, and every image and font has a recorded licence.
